μὲν παρὰ τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν, ὁτὲ δὲ παρὰ τὴν τροπολογίαν, καὶ ἔσθ' ὅτε παρὰ τὴν
σύμφρασιν ἀπαιτοῦσαν ἄλλως τῇ λέξει χρήσασθαι ἐν τοῖσδέ τισιν ἢ ὡς κεῖται ἐν
ἑτέροις. καὶ τοῦτο ἐὰν ἐπιμελῶς παραφυλατ τώμεθα, πολλῶν σφαλμάτων
ἀπαλλαττόμεθα καὶ παρεκδοχῶν. χρὴ οὖν εἰδέναι ὅτι τὸ ἑώρακεν οὐκ ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ
ἀεὶ κεῖται, ἀλλ' ὁτὲ μὲν ἐπὶ τοῦ σωματικοῦ ὁρᾷν, ὁτὲ δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ νοεῖν. καθόλου γὰρ
τοῦτο ἰστέον, ὅτι προκειμένου κρύψαι καὶ μὴ φανερῶς ἐκθέσθαι τὰ νοήματα τῆς
ἀληθείας τῷ ἐν τοῖς προφήταις πνεύματι καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις Χριστοῦ λόγῳ,
πολλαχοῦ καὶ ὑπὸ τῆς φράσεως συγχεῖται καὶ οὐχ ὡς ὑπὸ μίαν λέγεται ἀκολουθίαν·
ἵνα μὴ καὶ ἀνάξιοι εἰς κρίμα τῆς ἑαυτῶν ψυχῆς εὕρωσι τὰ συμφερόντως αὐτοῖς
ἀποκεκρυμμένα. καὶ τοῦτο πολλαχοῦ αἴτιόν ἐστι τοῦ δοκεῖν μὴ ἔχειν σύνταξιν μηδὲ
ἀκολουθίαν τὴν ὅλην γραφήν· καὶ μάλιστα, ὡς προείπομεν, τὴν προφη τικὴν καὶ
τὴν ἀποστολικήν· καὶ μάλιστα τῆς ἀποστολικῆς τὴν πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ἐπιστολήν, ἐν ᾗ
τὰ περὶ νόμου διαφόρως ὀνομάζεται, καὶ ἐπὶ διαφόρων πραγμάτων κείμενα· ὥστε
δοκεῖν ὅτι οὐκ ἔχεται ὁ Παῦλος ἐν τῇ γραφῇ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς τοῦ προκειμένου αὐτῷ
σκοποῦ.> 37 vii 7 τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία; μὴ γένοιτο· ἀλλὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν
οὐκ ἔγνων εἰ μὴ διὰ νόμου· τήν τε γὰρ ἐπιθυμίαν οὐκ ᾔδειν εἰ μὴ ὁ νόμος ἔλεγεν Οὐκ
ἐπιθυμήσεις. νόμον ὧδε νοοῦμεν οὐ μόνον τὸν Μωσέως τὸν κωλύοντα τὴν
ἐπιθυμίαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν φυσικόν· ἐνέσπαρται γὰρ ἡμῖν φυσικῶς ἡ ἐπιθυμία ὡς
πάθος, καὶ ὁ περὶ ταύτην νόμος, καὶ ἔλαβεν ἀφορμὴν ἡ ἁμαρτία οὐ διὰ τῆ γραπτῆς
μόνης ἐντολῆ , ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τῆς φυσικῆς. καὶ ὁ Ἀδὰμ δὲ ᾔδει τοῦτο καὶ πρὸ τοῦ
Μωσέως νόμου. 38 vii 8 ἀφορμὴν δὲ λαβοῦσα ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς
κατειργάσατο ἐν ἐμοὶ πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν. οὐκ ἐν Παύλῳ μόνῳ ἀλλ' ἐν πάσῃ ψυχῇ, ὅτε
ἡ ἁμαρτία ὑπέστη, πᾶσα ἐπιθυμία κατεπολέμει τὸ γένος· ἀμήχανον γὰρ ἀνθρωπίνην
ψυχὴν μὴ ὑπο πεσεῖν πάθεσι, κἂν ἐξ ἐπιμελείας ὕστερον οἱονεὶ ἐν ἀπαθείᾳ γένηται.
ὧδε δὲ ὁ Παῦλος πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν λέγει παθητικὴν καὶ ἁμαρτωλόν (ἣν ὁ νόμος
ἀπαγορεύει διδάσκων τὸ Οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις), ἥτις ἐστὶν ὄρεξις ἄλογος γινομένη κατὰ
ὁρμὴν πλεονάζουσαν παρὰ λόγον, καθ' ἣν φιλοζωοῦμεν, ὡς ἀγαθοῦ ὀρεγόμενοι τῆς
μέσης καὶ ἀδιαφόρου ζωῆς, προσκείμενοι πλούτῳ καὶ δόξῃ καὶ γυναιξὶ καὶ ταῖς
λοιπαῖς ἐπιθυμίαις, κατὰ τὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας βούλημα ποιούσης ἡμᾶς ἐκτείνεσθαι ὡς ἐπὶ
ἀγαθὸν <ἐπὶ> πᾶν τὸ ὑφ' ἡμῶν ἐπιθυ μούμενον. φαντασία γὰρ ἀγαθοῦ ἡ ἐπιθυμία
γίνεται. 39 vii 8–11 χωρὶς γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία νεκρά. ἐγὼ δὲ ἔζων χωρὶς νόμου ποτέ·
ἐλθούσης δὲ τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡ ἁμαρτία ἀνέζησεν, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπέθανον, καὶ εὑρέθη μοι ἡ
ἐντολὴ ἡ εἰς ζωὴν αὕτη εἰς θάνατον· ἡ γὰρ ἁμαρτία ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα διὰ τῆς
ἐντολῆς ἐξηπάτησέν με καὶ δι' αὐτῆς ἀπέκτεινεν. τότε γὰρ καὶ λέγοιτ' ἂν περὶ τοῦ
τοιούτου ὅτι οὗτος ζῇ χωρὶς νόμου· ἐπὶ ταύτην γὰρ τὴν κατάστασιν ἀναφέρων ὁ
Παῦλος καὶ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ἐρεῖ, ἐγὼ δὲ ἔζων χωρὶς νόμου ποτέ, ἐπεὶ ποτὲ ἦν χωρὶς
νόμου ὅπου, καθὼς αὐτός φησι, περιτομῇ ὀκταήμερο , ἐκ γένου Ἰ ραήλ, Ἑβραῖο ἐξ
Ἑβραίων· οὐ γὰρ δύναταιτὸ ἔτι ἄλογον ἔχον κατάστασιν παιδίον ζῇν ὑπὸ νόμον. πᾶς
γὰρ ἄνθρωπος ἔζη χωρὶς νόμου ποτέ, ὅτε παιδίον ἦν· <ὅτε οὐκ ἦν ἐπιτίμησις· ἄγνοια
γὰρ κολάσει οὐχ ὑπόκειται·> καὶ παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ ἦλθέν ποτε ἡ ἐντολή· πότε δὲ ἢ ὅτε
συνεπλήρωσε τὸν λόγον, καὶ νενόηκε τὴν ἐντολὴν προστάττουσαν μὲν τὰ τοιάδε,
ἀπαγορεύουσαν δὲ τὰ τοιάδε; ἅμα δὲ τῷ ἐλθεῖν τὴν ἐντολὴν κατὰ τὸν πρῶτον αὐτῆς
καιρὸν ὑφίσταται ἡ κακία, ἤ, ὡς ὁ Παῦλος ὠνόμασεν, ἀναζῇ ἡ ἁμαρτία τέως οὖσα
νεκρά· ἐπεὶ δὲ μὴ πέφυκεν ἅμα ζῇν ἁμαρτία καὶ ὁ ἔ ω ἄνθρωπο , διὰ τοῦτο ἐλθούσης
τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡ μὲν ἁμαρτία ἀναζῇ ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ ἀποθνήσκει, κατὰ τὸ ψυχὴ ἡ
ἁμαρτάνου α αὐτὴ ἀποθανεῖται. τὸ γὰρ ἐγὼ ἐπὶ τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν ἔ ω ἄνθρωπον
pass_a_gloss: Indeed, sometimes due to homonymy, sometimes due to tropology, and sometimes because the synthesis demands otherwise, we must use the word in these passages either as it stands or as it appears elsewhere; and if we carefully observe this, we escape many errors and conjectures. Therefore, we must know that what has been seen does not always lie in the same thing, but sometimes it is bodily seeing, sometimes instead of perceiving. For it must be known universally that when the purpose is to conceal and not clearly reveal the thoughts of the truth to the Spirit in the prophets and the Word of Christ in the apostles, in many places the phrasing confuses them and they are not spoken according to a single sequence, so that the unworthy may not come upon judgment against their own souls by finding what is secretly kept for their benefit. And this is often the cause of the opinion that the whole Scripture lacks syntax and sequence, especially, as we said before, the prophetic and apostolic writings, and most especially the apostolic letter to the Romans, in which the matters concerning the law are named differently and placed upon different things, so that it seems Paul does not hold to the purpose of the writing of the letter set before him. What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! But I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, 'You shall not covet.' Thus we understand the law not only as that of Moses forbidding covetousness, but also as the natural law; for the desire is naturally implanted in us as a passion, and the law concerning this, and sin has taken occasion not only through the written commandment, but also through the natural one. And Adam too knew this before the law of Moses. Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me all kinds of covetousness—not only in me, but in every soul when sin has arisen, all covetousness has warred against the race; for it is impossible for a human soul not to fall into passions, even if later, through care, it becomes, as it were, in impassibility. Thus Paul says all covetousness is passionate and sinful (which the law forbids by teaching 'You shall not covet'), and this is an irrational desire arising according to impulse, abounding beyond reason, by which we love life, as desiring good, the middle and indifferent life, attaching ourselves to wealth, glory, women, and other covetous things, doing the will of sin, causing us to stretch out as upon good upon all that we desire. For the fantasy of good becomes covetousness. Apart from the law, sin is dead. I once lived apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died, and I found that the very commandment intended for life became death to me; for sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Then it could be said of such a person that he lives apart from the law; for upon this condition, reflecting, Paul and every person would say, I once lived apart from the law, when, as he says, on the eighth day after birth, of the race of Israel, a Hebrew of the Hebrews; for it is not possible that an irrational infant, having a state, should live under law. Indeed, every person has lived apart from the law at some time, namely when they were a child, when there was no reproof, for ignorance is not subject to punishment; and the commandment has come at some time to every person; but when did they complete the word, and have understood the commandment enjoining such things and forbidding such things? And at the very moment the commandment came, according to its first time, wickedness arose, or, as Paul called it, sin awoke, being dead; for since it is not natural for sin and the human to live together, therefore, when the commandment came, sin awoke and the soul died, according to the soul, the sinning one, this one shall die. pass_b_english: At times we must interpret a word according to its plain meaning, at others figuratively, and occasionally because the context requires a different sense—either as it stands or as it appears elsewhere in Scripture. By observing this carefully, we avoid many mistakes and unfounded suppositions. Therefore, we must recognize that what has been perceived is not always located in the same reality; sometimes it is bodily sight, sometimes spiritual discernment. This principle must be universally understood: when the divine purpose is to conceal truth rather than reveal it openly to the Spirit in the prophets and to the Word of Christ in the apostles, the phrasing often becomes complex and does not follow a single, straightforward sequence. This is done so that the unworthy, upon encountering what is secretly reserved for their benefit, do not bring judgment upon themselves by seizing what was meant to remain hidden. This is frequently the reason why some suppose that Scripture as a whole lacks syntax and coherence—especially the prophetic and apostolic writings, and most notably Paul’s letter to the Romans, where legal matters are named differently and placed in varied contexts, making it seem as though Paul deviates from his stated purpose. But what shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness had the law not declared, 'You shall not covet.' Thus we understand the law not merely as Moses’ prohibition against covetousness, but also as the natural law ingrained in us—for desire is naturally implanted in us as a passion, and sin has seized opportunity not only through the written commandment but also through this inner law. Even Adam knew this before the Mosaic law. Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetousness—not only in me, but in every soul when sin awakens, all covetousness wages war against the human race; for it is impossible for a human soul not to fall into passions, even if later, through discipline, it appears, as it were, to attain impassibility. Paul declares that all covetousness is passionate and sinful—which the law forbids by teaching, 'You shall not covet'—and this is an irrational impulse arising from mere urge, overflowing beyond reason, by which we cling to life, desiring good, the middling and indifferent life, attaching ourselves to wealth, honor, women, and other covetous things, doing the will of sin, thus stretching ourselves toward what we imagine to be good upon all that we desire. For the fantasy of good becomes covetousness. Apart from the law, sin is powerless. I once lived apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died, and I found that the very commandment meant for life became death to me—for sin, seizing opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and thereby killed me. choices.choice: We must discern when to read figuratively and when literally, as the text demands, to avoid error.

choices.issue: the law's role in revealing sin
choices.choice: The law does not cause sin but reveals it, making known covetousness through its prohibition.
